messages.content: Write an internal post about making security everyone's responsibility at a software company. Around 250 words.

# Security is everyone's job, not just the security team's

Our security team reviews architecture, runs the vulnerability program, and responds when something breaks. They can't read every pull request, sit in every design meeting, or catch every misconfigured bucket. The people who write the code and run the infrastructure make most of the decisions that keep us safe, and that happens outside the security team's room.

A few habits matter more than any policy document.

Threat model your own feature before you ship it. Ask what happens if this input is malicious, this token leaks, or this service goes down. You know the feature better than anyone who reviews it later.

Treat a security finding like a bug, not an accusation. If someone flags an issue in your code, fix it. Don't defend the original design.

Report what looks wrong, even when you're not sure. A false alarm costs someone a few minutes. A real issue that goes unreported costs a lot more. Nobody here has ever caught grief for flagging something that turned out to be nothing.

Ask before you skip a control. If a security step slows you down, say so. Sometimes the control is outdated and needs to change. Sometimes it exists because of an incident nobody wants to repeat. Either way, raise it. Don't quietly route around it.

None of this replaces the security team's work. It changes what they're working with: fewer surprises, earlier signals, and problems caught while they're still cheap to fix.

If something concerns you, say something. That's the whole policy.

output:
# Security is everyone's job, not just the security team's

The security team reviews architecture, runs the vulnerability program, and shows up when something breaks. They can't read every pull request. They can't sit in every design meeting. They can't catch every misconfigured bucket. Most of the decisions that keep us safe happen outside their room, made by whoever's writing the code or running the infrastructure that day.

A few habits matter more than any policy document.

Threat model your own feature before you ship it. What happens if this input is malicious? If this token leaks? If this service goes down? You know the feature better than anyone who reviews it after the fact.

Treat a security finding like a bug, not an accusation. Someone flags an issue in your code, fix it. Skip the defense of the original design.

Report what looks wrong, even when you're not sure. A false alarm costs a few minutes. A real issue that goes unreported costs a lot more. Nobody here has caught grief for flagging something that turned out to be nothing.

Ask before you skip a control. If a step is slowing you down, say so out loud. Sometimes the control is outdated and needs to go. Sometimes it exists because of an incident nobody wants to live through twice. Either way, raise it — don't quietly route around it.

None of this replaces what the security team does. It changes what they're working with: fewer surprises, earlier signals, problems caught while they're still cheap to fix.

If something concerns you, say something. That's the whole policy.
